title: Publicizing Contract Actions: Synopsis, SAM.gov and Timing
summary: Publicizing is how the Government keeps the marketplace open, and it is a statutory duty, not a courtesy. The contracting officer posts the presolicitation notice, the solicitation and the award notice on the governmentwide point of entry at SAM.gov, observing the required waiting periods, unless one of the listed exemptions applies and is documented. Boards test the $25,000 award-notice threshold, the 15-day and 30-day waiting periods, the exemptions, and the combined synopsis and solicitation shortcut for commercial buys.

sections.heading: What must be publicized and where
sections.body:
The governmentwide point of entry is SAM.gov - the successor to FedBizOpps - and RFO FAR Part 5 requires the contracting officer to post there. Three postings carry the load:

- The presolicitation notice, historically called the synopsis, at RFO FAR 5.101. It tells industry a requirement is coming, what it is, and how to respond or express interest.
- The solicitation itself at RFO FAR 5.201, with content requirements at 5.201(c) including the point of contact and the response instructions.
- The award notice at RFO FAR 5.301 for contract actions exceeding $25,000, and a public announcement at RFO FAR 5.302 for awards over $5.5 million, which is coordinated through public affairs and congressional notification channels.

The purposes stated in the FAR are worth quoting on a board: increase competition, broaden industry participation in meeting Government requirements, and assist small business concerns in obtaining contracts and subcontracts.

sections.heading: The timing rules
sections.body:
The waiting periods are the most-tested facts in this topic. Under the RFO the timing tables sit at 5.101(d) for the presolicitation notice and 5.201(d) for the solicitation, and they run from 10 to 45 days depending on the dollar value and whether a trade agreement applies. The classic sequence, which the question bank still teaches, is:

- Post the presolicitation notice at least 15 days before issuing the solicitation.
- Allow at least a 30-day response time for receipt of offers from the date the solicitation is issued, for proposed contract actions expected to exceed $25,000.
- For commercial products and services, the KO may set a shorter reasonable response period, and for acquisitions subject to a trade agreement the longer periods apply.

What a board wants is not the table memorized but the discipline: I confirm the applicable period on the current 5.101(d) and 5.201(d) tables, I build the schedule backward from the required award date, and I do not compress a statutory waiting period to make a customer's suspense - I get a documented authority or I move the date.

sections.heading: Exemptions from the presolicitation notice
sections.body:
RFO FAR 5.101(b) carries the exemptions (legacy FAR 5.202). Name several and say that each must be documented in the file.

- Unusual and compelling urgency, where the Government would be seriously injured by the delay.
- The posting would compromise national security.
- The contract action is made under the simplified procedures for micro-purchases, or otherwise below the notice threshold.
- The action is an order placed under an existing indefinite-delivery contract, a Federal Supply Schedule, or a required source under Part 8.
- Utility services where only one source is available.
- Perishable subsistence, or actions where performance can only be by a source under an international agreement.
- The action is for a brand-name commercial item for authorized resale, or the logical follow-on rules apply.

The honest board answer names three or four accurately, then says the full list is at RFO FAR 5.101(b) and that an exemption is a documented decision, not an assumption. A synopsis exemption does not excuse competition - it excuses the notice, and I still need a Part 6 authority if I am restricting competition.

sections.heading: Combined synopsis and solicitation
sections.body:
For commercial products and commercial services the contracting officer may use a combined synopsis and solicitation - one posting that serves as both the notice and the solicitation - under RFO FAR 12.202(b), the RFO home of the legacy FAR 12.603 procedure.

How it works and what it buys you:

- The single notice contains the information a synopsis would contain plus the solicitation terms, the provisions and clauses incorporated by reference, and the evaluation basis.
- It eliminates the separate 15-day wait between the notice and the solicitation, so it shortens the cycle materially.
- It still has to allow a reasonable response time, and the reasonable-time judgment is the KO's and must fit the complexity of the requirement.
- It is limited to commercial acquisitions - do not use it on a noncommercial buy to save time.

This is a frequent board question in exactly that form: under the old FAR 12.603, what procedure may the KO use when a written solicitation will be issued for a commercial item? The answer is the combined synopsis and solicitation, now at RFO FAR 12.202(b).

sections.heading: Synopsis, sole source and the pre-award notices
sections.body:
Publicizing interacts with competition. Two connections a board likes:

- When you intend to award without full and open competition, the presolicitation notice is still generally required, and the notice itself is one of the things that tests your market assumption. A sole-source notice that draws three capable responses means your market research was wrong; that is a feature, not a failure. Keep the notice period open and actually read the responses before you sign the justification and approval under RFO FAR 6.104.
- Brand-name restrictions require the justification and the notice to state the brand-name basis (RFO FAR 6.103-1(d) and 11.204), and the notice content requirement at RFO FAR 5.201(c)(3) carries the disclosure.

Also know the preaward and postaward notice obligations that live in Part 15: preaward notices to unsuccessful offerors excluded from the competitive range at RFO FAR 15.206-1, preaward debriefings at 15.206-2, and postaward debriefings at 15.301. Those are notices to offerors, distinct from the Part 5 public postings, and mixing them up is a common candidate error.

sections.heading: How boards probe publicizing
sections.body:
The standard opener is flat recall: when are you required to synopsize, and what about the award? Answer with the $25,000 threshold for the award notice, the presolicitation notice before solicitation, the 15-day and 30-day sequence, and SAM.gov as the governmentwide point of entry.

Then the follow-ups:

- Name exemptions. Give three or four real ones and point to RFO FAR 5.101(b).
- The customer needs award in ten days. What do you do? Do not skip the notice. Options are a documented urgency exemption with the corresponding Part 6 authority and justification, a commercial combined synopsis and solicitation with a reasonable but short response time, an order under an existing contract, or a bridge under the right authority - each with its own approval.
- Who can waive the waiting period? Nobody in the field waives a statutory period; the KO applies an exemption that exists or accepts the schedule.
- What happens if you get it wrong? A protest ground, a competition advocate finding, and an award at risk.

The theme: publicizing is the Government's promise to the market, and the KO keeps it or documents why the rule does not apply.

Solicitation notice content (legacy FAR 5.102(a)(6)); timing table at 5.201(d).

board_angles.q: When are you required to synopsize a contract action?
board_angles.a: For proposed contract actions expected to exceed $25,000 I post a presolicitation notice on SAM.gov before issuing the solicitation, and I post an award notice for actions exceeding $25,000 - unless an exemption at RFO FAR 5.101(b) applies and is documented.

board_angles.q: What is the timing between the synopsis, the solicitation and award?
board_angles.a: The classic sequence is the presolicitation notice at least 15 days before the solicitation issues and at least a 30-day response period for offers, with the current tables at RFO FAR 5.101(d) and 5.201(d) running from 10 to 45 days depending on dollar value and trade agreement coverage - I confirm the applicable period and build the schedule backward from it.

board_angles.q: Name some exceptions to the synopsis requirement.
board_angles.a: Unusual and compelling urgency, postings that would compromise national security, micro-purchases and other actions below the threshold, orders under existing indefinite-delivery or Federal Supply Schedule contracts, utility services with only one source, and perishable subsistence - the full list is at RFO FAR 5.101(b) and each use is documented.

board_angles.q: You are buying a commercial service and the schedule is tight. What tool do you use?
board_angles.a: A combined synopsis and solicitation under RFO FAR 12.202(b) - one SAM.gov posting that serves as both notice and solicitation with a reasonable response period, which removes the separate 15-day wait but does not remove my obligation to give industry a fair chance to respond.

board_angles.q: Your customer says the requirement is urgent and asks you to skip the synopsis. Your answer?
board_angles.a: I do not skip it on a customer's say-so - either an exemption at RFO FAR 5.101(b) genuinely applies and I document it along with the corresponding Part 6 authority and justification at 6.104, or the schedule moves; an unjustified failure to publicize is a protest ground and puts the award at risk.

board_angles.q: Where do preaward and postaward debriefings fit in publicizing?
board_angles.a: They do not - those are notices to offerors under Part 15 at RFO FAR 15.206-1, 15.206-2 and 15.301, separate from the public SAM.gov postings required by Part 5.

title: Contract Administration: CORs, Modifications and the Changes Clause
summary: After award the contracting officer is the only person who can change the contract, and everything else in administration flows from protecting that line. The COR is the KO's designated eyes and ears for technical surveillance with no authority to direct changes, commit funds, or alter the terms. Modifications are either bilateral, signed by both parties, or unilateral under a clause that authorizes the KO to act alone - and the Changes clause is the one that requires the contractor to keep working while the money is sorted out.

sections.heading: COR designation and limits
sections.body:
A COR is designated in writing by the contracting officer to perform technical monitoring and surveillance - the KO's eyes and ears, not a second contracting officer. Under DFARS 201.404-70 and its PGI a COR must be designated for service contracts, and in practice for any contract where surveillance is needed, nominated by the requiring activity as early as practicable in the acquisition process.

The designation letter is the whole game. It states:

- The specific authorities delegated and the limits - inspect and accept for the Government where delegated, monitor performance, review invoices for technical sufficiency, maintain a COR file.
- What the COR may never do: change the price, quantity, quality, delivery schedule, period of performance or any other term; authorize work outside the scope; direct the contractor's employees; obligate funds; or make any commitment affecting cost.
- The training and certification the COR must hold, the appointment effective date, and the requirement to report to the KO.

A COR who directs a change creates an unauthorized commitment, ratifiable only under RFO FAR 1.405 if at all. Say the sentence on the board: the COR has no authority to change the contract.

sections.heading: Post-award orientation
sections.body:
The post-award orientation conference - the start-of-work meeting - exists to make sure the contractor and the Government have the same understanding of the contract before anyone spends money. RFO FAR 42.302(a)(3) lists conducting post-award orientation conferences among the contract administration functions.

What to cover: the scope and the deliverables; the QASP and how surveillance will run; invoicing and payment procedures including who certifies receipt; security, access and installation requirements - which overseas means SOFA status, base access and any invited contractor processing; government-furnished property and information; the key personnel and the points of contact on both sides; the COR's authority and its limits, said out loud in front of the contractor; how changes are requested and who may authorize them; and reporting requirements.

What is inappropriate: renegotiating price or terms; directing work beyond the contract; letting the customer give the contractor a to-do list; anything that creates an expectation of extra work. The orientation clarifies the contract; it does not amend it. If something surfaces that genuinely needs to change, that is a modification action afterward, signed by the KO.

sections.heading: Modifications: bilateral, unilateral and administrative
sections.body:
A contract modification is any written change in the terms of the contract, and RFO FAR Part 43 governs.

- Bilateral modification, a supplemental agreement, is signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer. Use it to definitize a change order, to reflect a negotiated equitable adjustment, to incorporate a settlement, or to make any change that requires the contractor's consent. It is the preferred vehicle because it closes out the price and the schedule at the same time as the change.
- Unilateral modification is signed only by the contracting officer. Use it to make administrative changes, to issue change orders under the Changes clause, to issue termination notices, and to exercise options under an option clause. The authority must come from a clause already in the contract.
- Administrative change is a unilateral modification that does not affect the substantive rights of the parties - a change in the paying office, an appropriation data correction, an address change.

On the board, when handed a scenario, say which type and which clause gives you the authority. A modification with no clause authority and no contractor signature is not a modification - it is a problem.

sections.heading: Scope: the question before every modification
sections.body:
Before you touch a modification, ask whether the change is within the scope of the contract. If it is outside the scope, it is a new procurement requiring its own competition or a justified sole-source authority under Part 6 - you cannot buy new work under an old contract.

The test courts and GAO apply: would the modified work be materially different from the work competed? Look at whether the solicitation put offerors on notice that this kind of change could occur, the magnitude relative to the original effort, whether the nature or type of work changes, and whether other firms would have competed differently.

- Within scope: a quantity change inside the stated variation, a design refinement under the Changes clause, a period adjustment consistent with the terms.
- Outside scope: adding a new line of work, a major increase in quantity beyond what was competed, a change of the end item.

A cardinal change - so far outside scope it is effectively a new contract - is both protest exposure and potential breach. Document the scope analysis and bring in counsel before signing.

sections.heading: The Changes clause and the duty to proceed
sections.body:
The Changes clauses at RFO FAR 52.243-1 through 52.243-7 give the contracting officer the unilateral right to make changes within the general scope of the contract - in the drawings, designs or specifications; in the method of shipment or packing; in the place of delivery; and for services, in the description of services or the place of performance.

The rules a board wants:

- Only the contracting officer may issue a change order. Anyone else's direction is a constructive change at best and an unauthorized commitment at worst.
- If the change causes an increase or decrease in cost or in the time required for performance, the KO must make an equitable adjustment and modify the contract.
- The contractor must assert its right to an adjustment within the period stated in the clause, normally 30 days from receipt of the change order, though the KO may consider a late assertion at any time before final payment.
- RFO FAR 43.301(b) and the clause require the contractor to continue performance as changed while the adjustment is negotiated. Disagreement over money is not a stop-work authority, and stop-work is a separate clause.

sections.heading: Requests for equitable adjustment and claims
sections.body:
A request for equitable adjustment is the contractor asking for more money or time under a clause of the contract - Changes, Government Delay of Work, Differing Site Conditions, Suspension of Work, Government Property. It is not automatically a claim.

My process:

- Acknowledge receipt and get the REA in writing with the specific clause relied on, the factual basis, and a cost breakdown by element.
- Determine entitlement first, then quantum. Is there a compensable change, did the Government cause it, and does a clause give relief? If entitlement fails, no amount of cost detail matters.
- For DoD, the REA certification at DFARS 252.243-7002 applies above the stated threshold - the contractor certifies the request is made in good faith and the supporting data are accurate and complete.
- Analyze cost with proposal rigor - cost analysis, audit support if the dollars warrant, and the Part 31 cost principles.
- Negotiate and definitize by bilateral modification with a release of claims.
- If it arrives as a certified claim over $100,000 under the Contract Disputes Act, the clock runs and appeal rights attach.

Contract Administration and Audit Services - part page.
Conduct post-award orientation conferences - contract administration function.
Contract Modifications - part page.

Changes - Fixed-Price; the Changes clause family runs 52.243-1 through 52.243-7.
Ratification of unauthorized commitments (legacy FAR 1.602-3).
Requests for equitable adjustment - contractor certification.

board_angles.q: What is the role of your COR and what can they not do?
board_angles.a: The COR is my designated technical eyes and ears - surveillance under the QASP, invoice review for technical sufficiency, documentation and reporting - and they may never change price, quantity, quality, schedule or any term, direct contractor employees, obligate funds, or authorize work outside the scope.

board_angles.q: When would you use a bilateral versus a unilateral modification?
board_angles.a: Bilateral when the change needs the contractor's consent - definitizing a change order, a negotiated equitable adjustment, a settlement; unilateral when a clause already in the contract gives me the authority to act alone - administrative changes, change orders under the Changes clause, option exercises and termination notices.

board_angles.q: How do you determine whether a change is within scope?
board_angles.a: I ask whether the modified work is materially different from what was competed - whether the solicitation put offerors on notice that this kind of change could occur, the magnitude relative to the original effort, and whether other firms would have competed differently; if it is outside scope it is a new procurement needing competition or a Part 6 justification.

board_angles.q: You issue a unilateral change order and the contractor disagrees with the price. What must the contractor do?
board_angles.a: Continue performance as changed - RFO FAR 43.301(b) and the Changes clause impose a duty to proceed - while asserting its right to an equitable adjustment within the period stated in the clause, normally 30 days, and we negotiate the adjustment and definitize by bilateral modification.

board_angles.q: What is the purpose of the post-award orientation, and what is inappropriate there?
board_angles.a: To align both parties on the contract as written - scope, deliverables, surveillance, invoicing, access and property, and the COR's limits stated in front of the contractor; it is inappropriate to renegotiate price or terms, to direct work beyond the contract, or to let the customer hand the contractor a to-do list.

board_angles.q: A contractor hands you an REA. Walk me through your process.
board_angles.a: Get it in writing with the clause relied on, the facts and a cost breakdown; decide entitlement before quantum; obtain the DFARS 252.243-7002 certification where required; analyze cost against the Part 31 cost principles with audit support if the dollars warrant; negotiate and definitize by bilateral modification with a release - and if it arrives as a certified claim over $100,000, I run the Contract Disputes Act clock and issue a final decision.

title: Terminations: Convenience, Default and the Commercial Path
summary: The Government holds a unique right to terminate a contract for its own convenience, and a separate right to terminate for the contractor's failure to perform. Termination for convenience buys out the contractor's incurred costs and profit on work done; termination for default is a drastic sanction that requires a documented failure, consideration of excusable causes, and usually a cure or show-cause notice first. Commercial contracts follow a shorter path under RFO FAR 12.304 with termination for cause rather than default.

sections.heading: Termination for convenience
sections.body:
Termination for convenience is exercised when it is in the Government's interest - the requirement went away, funding changed, the mission changed, or a protest corrective action requires it. It is a unilateral action taken by the contracting officer under the Termination for Convenience clause, and the contractor's remedy is a settlement rather than breach damages.

What the contractor gets:

- The contract price for completed and accepted items.
- Costs incurred on the terminated work, including a reasonable allowance for settlement expenses and subcontractor settlements.
- Profit on work actually performed. Under RFO FAR 49.202, profit is allowed on preparations made and work done, but never on the terminated - that is, unperformed - portion, and no anticipatory profit and no consequential damages are allowed. If the contract would have been a loss contract, a loss adjustment applies and profit is denied.

Process: issue the notice stating the effective date and extent; direct the contractor to stop work and preserve property; instruct on subcontract terminations; negotiate the settlement proposal. Partial terminations are common and the surviving work may need an equitable adjustment.

sections.heading: Termination for default - and what to do first
sections.body:
Termination for default is available when the contractor fails to deliver on time, fails to make progress so as to endanger performance, or fails to perform any other material provision. It is a drastic sanction. Before I sign one I consider the factors the FAR directs: the terms of the contract and the specific failure; the specific failure's effect on the Government; the availability of the supplies or services from other sources and the time to get them; the urgency of the need and the period that would be required to obtain them elsewhere; the degree of essentiality of the contractor in the Government's acquisition program and the effect on its ability to supply other contractors; the contractor's capability and whether a different approach would produce performance; the effect on the contractor's ability to liquidate progress payments; and any excusable cause.

I also coordinate with counsel, with the requiring activity on the impact, with the small business specialist if the contractor is small, and with my chain - a default that is later converted by a board or court to a termination for convenience costs the Government the settlement anyway plus the delay.

sections.heading: Cure notices and show cause notices
sections.body:
The delinquency notices are at RFO FAR 49.607 and boards ask about the ten-day rule almost every time.

- Cure notice: used when the failure is something other than a failure to deliver on time - for example, failure to make progress or failure to perform a material provision - and there is still delivery time remaining. It gives the contractor 10 days, or longer if the KO allows, to cure the condition. Before issuing it, confirm that a period at least equal to the cure period remains in the delivery schedule. If less than 10 days remain, do not issue a cure notice.
- Show cause notice: used when the time remaining is insufficient for a cure period, or when the delivery date has already passed. It tells the contractor the Government is considering termination for default and asks it to show cause why it should not be terminated, including any excusable causes, so that the KO has the facts before deciding.

Neither notice is a termination; both build the record and preserve the Government's position. Send by a method that documents receipt, and if the response establishes an excusable cause the answer is an extension, not a default.

sections.heading: Excusable delay
sections.body:
An excusable delay is a failure to perform arising from causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor. The Excusable Delays clause at RFO FAR 52.249-14 and the default clauses list the classic causes: acts of God or of the public enemy; acts of the Government in either its sovereign or contractual capacity; fires; floods; epidemics; quarantine restrictions; strikes; freight embargoes; and unusually severe weather.

Rules that matter:

- The delay must be beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence. A subcontractor delay is excusable only if the cause would be excusable for the prime and the items were not obtainable elsewhere in time.
- The remedy is normally a no-cost time extension, not money. Money comes only if a clause such as Government Delay of Work or Suspension of Work provides it.
- An excusable delay defeats a termination for default, which is why the show cause notice asks for it.

Handed a no-cost time extension request, say: I evaluate whether the cause is excusable under the clause, and if it is I extend the schedule by bilateral modification at no cost.

sections.heading: Commercial terminations under 12.304
sections.body:
Commercial contracts do not use Part 49 mechanics. RFO FAR 12.304 and the commercial terms clause give two routes.

- Termination for the Government's convenience: the Government pays the percentage of the contract price reflecting the percentage of work performed prior to the notice, plus reasonable charges the contractor can demonstrate from its records - and the standard is what a prudent commercial party would pay, not a Part 49 settlement proposal with cost accounting detail.
- Termination for cause: the commercial analogue to default. The Government may terminate for cause when the contractor fails to comply with contract terms or fails to provide adequate assurance of future performance. The contractor is liable to the Government for any excess reprocurement costs and the Government retains its rights for nonconforming items.

Part 49 may be used as guidance for the commercial case where it does not conflict with Part 12 and the clause. A cure or show cause notice is not required by the commercial clause, but sending one builds the record and is what a reasonable buyer would do.

sections.heading: After a default - the contractor's liabilities and the KO's next moves
sections.body:
RFO FAR 49.402-2 sets out the effect of a termination for default on a fixed-price contract.

- The Government is not liable for the contractor's costs on undelivered work and is entitled to repayment of any advance and progress payments applicable to that work.
- The Government may require the contractor to transfer title and deliver completed supplies, manufacturing materials and work in process, and pay the fair value of what it takes.
- The contractor is liable to the Government for any excess costs incurred in reprocuring supplies or services similar to those terminated - the reprocurement must be at a reasonable price and within a reasonable time, and the KO should document the reasonableness because the excess costs will be challenged.
- The Government may collect against the performance bond where one exists, and may assess liquidated damages where the clause provides for them.

Other consequences: the default is reported in CPARS and FAPIIS and follows the firm into future responsibility determinations; the contractor may appeal under the Contract Disputes Act; and an improper default converts to a convenience termination. That conversion risk is why the notice step, the excusable-cause analysis and legal review are not optional.

Effect of termination for default - excess reprocurement costs, repayment of advance and progress payments, title transfer.

Delinquency notices - cure notice and show cause notice, with the 10-day cure period.
Commercial terminations - convenience and for cause.

board_angles.q: Describe the different types of terminations available.
board_angles.a: For noncommercial contracts, termination for convenience when it is in the Government's interest with a cost-based settlement, and termination for default for failure to deliver, failure to make progress or failure to perform a material provision; for commercial contracts, RFO FAR 12.304 gives termination for the Government's convenience paying the percentage of work performed plus demonstrable charges, and termination for cause with excess reprocurement cost liability.

board_angles.q: When do you issue a cure notice versus a show cause notice?
board_angles.a: A cure notice when the failure is other than late delivery and at least 10 days of the delivery schedule remain, giving the contractor 10 days to cure; a show cause notice when insufficient time remains or the delivery date has passed, asking the contractor to show cause why it should not be terminated for default and to state any excusable causes.

board_angles.q: What factors do you consider before terminating for default?
board_angles.a: The specific failure and the contract terms, the effect on the Government, availability of the supplies or services from other sources and the time to get them, the urgency and essentiality of the requirement, the contractor's capability and whether another approach would work, the effect on progress payment liquidation, and above all whether the failure is excusable.

board_angles.q: Define an excusable delay and what the contractor gets for it.
board_angles.a: A failure to perform arising from causes beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence - acts of God, acts of the Government, fires, floods, epidemics, quarantine, strikes, embargoes, unusually severe weather - and the normal remedy is a no-cost time extension by bilateral modification, not money, unless a delay clause provides compensation.

board_angles.q: Where is profit allowed and not allowed on a fixed-price termination for convenience?
board_angles.a: Profit is allowed on preparations made and work actually performed, and it is not allowed on the terminated unperformed portion - no anticipatory profit and no consequential damages, and if the contract would have been a loss contract a loss adjustment denies profit entirely.

board_angles.q: What additional liabilities does the contractor incur after a termination for default?
board_angles.a: The Government owes nothing for undelivered work and can recover advance and progress payments applicable to it, can take title to completed supplies and work in process at fair value, and the contractor is liable for the excess costs of reprocuring similar supplies or services - plus the default record follows the firm into future responsibility determinations.

title: Protests: Agency, GAO and the Court of Federal Claims
summary: A protest is a written objection to a solicitation or an award, and a disappointed offeror has three forums: me as the contracting officer, the Government Accountability Office, or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. What changes between forums is speed, cost, who decides, and whether performance stops automatically. Know the clocks, know who signs the override, and never decide a protest alone.

sections.heading: The three forums and what each one buys the protester
sections.body:
All three live in RFO FAR Subpart 33.1.

- Agency protest, RFO FAR 33.104. Filed with me, or the protester may ask for an independent review at a level above me. Fastest and cheapest; the agency uses best efforts to resolve it in 35 days. No filing fee, no discovery, and I can take corrective action the same week.
- GAO protest, RFO FAR 33.105, under the Competition in Contracting Act at 31 U.S.C. 3551-3556 and GAO's own rules at 4 CFR Part 21. A neutral forum, a written decision in 100 days, and the automatic stay if the protest is timely.
- Court of Federal Claims, RFO FAR 33.106, under the Tucker Act at 28 U.S.C. 1491(b). Real litigation before a judge. There is no automatic stay; the protester must win an injunction. No time bar comparable to GAO's, and the court can hear a protest GAO has already denied.

A protester who loses at the agency still has 10 days from initial adverse agency action to get to GAO.

sections.heading: Timeliness: the clocks that decide most protests
sections.body:
Boards love this because timeliness disposes of more protests than the merits do.

- Solicitation improprieties apparent on the face of the solicitation must be protested before the closing date for receipt of proposals (agency rule at RFO FAR 33.104-2; GAO rule at 4 CFR 21.2(a)(1)).
- All other grounds: within 10 days after the basis is known or should have been known (4 CFR 21.2(a)(2)).
- Where a debriefing is requested and required, within 10 days after the debriefing is held.
- Agency-to-GAO: within 10 days of initial adverse agency action (4 CFR 21.2(a)(3)).
- The stay clocks are separate and shorter: a postaward protest must reach the agency or GAO within 10 days after award, or 5 days after the debriefing date offered under a timely request, whichever is later.

Days are calendar days; a deadline landing on a weekend or federal holiday rolls to the next business day. Timely for the stay and timely for the protest are two different tests - say both out loud.

sections.heading: The CICA stay and the override finding
sections.body:
The stay is statutory, not discretionary. Preaward: if GAO notifies the agency before award, I may not award (RFO FAR 33.105-2; 31 U.S.C. 3553(c)). Postaward: if GAO notice arrives within 10 days of award or 5 days after the offered debriefing date, whichever is later, I must immediately suspend performance or terminate the award (RFO FAR 33.105-3; 31 U.S.C. 3553(d)). In practice that means a stop-work order under FAR 52.242-15 the same day.

The override is the head of the contracting activity's alone and is nondelegable. Preaward it takes a written finding of urgent and compelling circumstances significantly affecting the interests of the United States, plus a finding that award is likely within 30 days. Postaward the HCA may find urgent and compelling circumstances or that performance is in the best interests of the Government. GAO must be notified of the finding. The agency-level equivalent is at RFO FAR 33.104-2(b)(1) and 33.104-3; it is still a written finding, not an assumption.

Override findings are themselves protestable at the Court of Federal Claims. Say that.

sections.heading: Running a GAO protest: the agency report and the decision
sections.body:
GAO notifies the agency within one day of filing. My first call is legal counsel, as RFO FAR 33.105-4 requires, then my chief and the SCO; in the 411th the supporting legal office and C&P route it into the ACC and Army legal channel.

Same day: notify the awardee (4 CFR 21.3(a)), put a litigation hold on the file and the evaluators' notes, run the timeliness test, and issue the stop-work order if the stay applies. Then take an honest look at whether the protester has a point - corrective action on day two costs far less than a sustained protest on day ninety.

The agency report is due to GAO 30 days after notice (4 CFR 21.3(c)) and contains the contracting officer's statement of facts, a legal memorandum, and the relevant documents. The protester comments within 10 days. GAO decides within 100 days of filing, or 65 days under the express option (4 CFR 21.9, 21.10). GAO's recommendation is not binding, but if the agency does not implement it within 60 days the head of the procuring activity must report that to GAO (RFO FAR 33.105-4(b); 31 U.S.C. 3554(e)).

sections.heading: Task-order protests and the DoD dollar floor
sections.body:
Orders under multiple-award contracts are mostly protest-proof, with two exceptions: a protest that the order increases the scope, period or maximum value of the underlying contract, and a protest at GAO of an order over the statutory dollar floor. GAO's jurisdiction over those is exclusive (RFO FAR 16.508, legacy 16.505(a)(10)).

The numbers in regulations.json: the DoD, NASA and Coast Guard floor is $35,000,000, raised from $25 million by FY2025 NDAA section 885(f) and carried in DFARS 252.216-7010(b)(1) under DoD Class Deviation 2026-O0045 Rev. 1. The civilian-agency floor is $10,000,000 (41 U.S.C. 4106(f)).

This is a live trap: parts of the bank and older study decks still say $25 million. If a board member uses $25 million, answer with the current figure, name the NDAA change, and offer to confirm it. Two related numbers worth carrying: fair-opportunity enhanced procedures kick in above $7,500,000 (RFO FAR 16.507-5), and DoD postaward debriefings are required on orders of $15,000,000 or more.

sections.heading: How boards probe this
sections.body:
The board is testing whether you will stop performance when you are supposed to and whether you know the limit of your own signature. Expect a fact pattern with a date in it, and expect the follow-up to move the date by two days to see whether the stay still applies.

The answer that scores well does four things in order: names the forum, applies the timeliness test to the facts you were given, states what happens to performance and who signs any override, then says what you do in the first 24 hours - legal, notify the awardee, litigation hold, consider corrective action.

Things that score a 1: confusing the 35-day agency best-effort rule with the 100-day GAO decision period; saying you would override the stay yourself; treating a vague objection letter as not a protest without asking legal (see Q0160); citing FAR 33.103 or 33.104 for GAO, which is pre-RFO numbering. Boards also like the closing question from Q0055: without competitive prejudice, no protest is sustained, no matter what the agency did wrong.

Postaward agency protest: suspend performance if filed within 10 days after award or 5 days after an offered debriefing, whichever is later, unless continued performance is justified in writing.

Protests to GAO; 33.105-2 preaward stay, 33.105-3 postaward stay and nondelegable HCA override, 33.105-4 other procedures including notify legal counsel and the 60-day report to GAO. Pre-RFO this was 33.104.
Protests to the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. No automatic stay; injunctive relief under 28 U.S.C. 1491(b).
GAO Bid Protest Regulations: 21.2 timeliness, 21.3 notice to the awardee and the 30-day agency report, 21.9 the 100-day decision, 21.10 the 65-day express option. Unchanged by the RFO.
CICA. 3553(c) preaward stay, 3553(d) postaward stay and the HCA override findings, 3554(a) the 100-day and 65-day periods, 3554(e) the report when a recommendation is not followed.

Task and delivery order protest limits (legacy 16.505(a)(10)). DoD floor $35,000,000 per 10 U.S.C. 3406(f)(1)(B) as amended by FY2025 NDAA sec. 885(f); civilian floor $10,000,000 per 41 U.S.C. 4106(f).
DoD: the 5-day stay clock runs from the conclusion of the enhanced postaward debriefing, including the follow-up question period.

board_angles.q: What are the three forums for a bid protest and what is the practical difference?
board_angles.a: Agency under RFO FAR 33.104 - fastest, 35-day best effort, I or an official above me decide; GAO under 33.105 - 100-day decision, automatic CICA stay if timely; Court of Federal Claims under 33.106 - a judge, no automatic stay, injunction required.

board_angles.q: A GAO protest is filed four days after award. What happens to performance and who can change that?
board_angles.a: The stay applies, so I immediately suspend performance with a stop-work order under 52.242-15; only the head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, can override it with a written urgent-and-compelling or best-interest finding, and GAO must be told.

board_angles.q: How long does the agency have to decide an agency-level protest?
board_angles.a: There is no statutory deadline, but RFO FAR 33.104-4(c)(1) requires best efforts to resolve it within 35 days of receipt by me or by the independent-review official.

board_angles.q: What is the GAO jurisdictional floor for a DoD task order protest?
board_angles.a: $35 million for DoD, NASA and the Coast Guard since the FY2025 NDAA raised it from $25 million; $10 million for civilian agencies - plus GAO always hears a protest that the order exceeds the scope, period or maximum value of the contract.

board_angles.q: What is in the agency report and when is it due?
board_angles.a: The contracting officer's statement of facts, a legal memorandum and the relevant record, due to GAO 30 days after notice under 4 CFR 21.3(c); the protester comments 10 days later and GAO decides within 100 days.

board_angles.q: An unsuccessful offeror sends an angry letter that never uses the word protest. What do you do?
board_angles.a: I send it to legal the same day for an opinion on whether it is a protest, preserve the file, and do not start the clock or dismiss it on my own reading of the words.

The $35M DoD task-order floor comes from the verified thresholds entry. title: Claims and Disputes Under the CDA
summary: A claim is a written demand, as a matter of right, for a sum certain or other contract relief - and almost everything a contractor sends me is not one until it is. The Contract Disputes Act gives the contractor a path from request to my final decision to the ASBCA or the Court of Federal Claims, and it puts interest on the Government's meter from the day I receive a proper claim. My job is to know when the clock starts, to decide rather than to stall, and to keep the file good enough that somebody else can defend it.

sections.heading: What is a claim, and what is not
sections.body:
A claim is a written demand or written assertion by one of the contracting parties seeking, as a matter of right, the payment of money in a sum certain, the adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief arising under or relating to the contract.

Three words do the work. Written - a phone call or a hallway complaint is never a claim. As a matter of right - not a request for a favor. Sum certain - a specific number, not "we think we are owed something in the range of."

What is not a claim: a voucher, invoice or routine request for payment that is not in dispute when submitted. It can become one by written notice to the contracting officer if it is disputed as to liability or amount, or if it is not acted on in a reasonable time.

Either party can claim. A Government demand for money - defective work, overpayment, liquidated damages - is a claim too, and it also requires a contracting officer's final decision. Boards like that reversal; be ready for it.

sections.heading: REA or claim: the distinction that costs money
sections.body:
A request for equitable adjustment is a business proposal for more money or time under a contract clause - Changes, Government Delay of Work, Suspension of Work, Differing Site Conditions. It is negotiated. It does not require certification, it does not start CDA interest, and there is no 60-day decision deadline.

A claim is a legal demand. It triggers certification over the threshold, CDA interest, my duty to issue a final decision, and the contractor's right to appeal.

The practical sequence: the contractor submits an REA, we negotiate, and if we cannot settle, the contractor converts it to a claim in writing. Most disputes should never get past the REA stage. When an REA arrives I notify legal, evaluate merit, negotiate, and use ADR through legal if negotiation stalls - ADR is available before or after my final decision.

The trap is the e-mail that says "we think we are owed another $150,000." Is that a claim? Not yet - it lacks the demand as a matter of right and, depending on wording, a sum certain. Say why, and say what would make it one.

sections.heading: Certification and the six-year limit
sections.body:
A contractor claim exceeding $100,000 is not a claim under 41 U.S.C. chapter 71 until it is certified. The certificate states that the claim is made in good faith, that the supporting data are accurate and complete to the best of the contractor's knowledge and belief, that the amount accurately reflects the contract adjustment for which the contractor believes the Government is liable, and that the certifier is authorized to certify on the contractor's behalf.

The threshold value is in regulations.json: $100,000, at RFO FAR 33.205-2 and the Disputes clause 52.233-1(d), implementing 41 U.S.C. 7103(b).

Two nuances boards probe. First, a defective certification is curable and does not stop interest from running (41 U.S.C. 7103(b)(3)); a complete absence of certification is jurisdictional and I should return the submission and say why. Second, aggregation - a contractor cannot split one claim into pieces under $100,000 to dodge certification.

Each claim must be submitted to the contracting officer within six years after accrual (41 U.S.C. 7103(a)(4)). Accrual is when all events fixing liability were known or should have been known.

sections.heading: The contracting officer's final decision
sections.body:
For a claim of $100,000 or less, I issue a written decision within 60 days of receiving a written request for a decision. For a claim over $100,000, within 60 days I either issue the decision or notify the contractor of a firm date by which I will - and that date must be reasonable given the size and complexity.

The decision has to contain a description of the claim, a statement of the factual areas of agreement and disagreement, a statement of the decision with supporting rationale, the paragraph that tells the contractor about its appeal rights to the agency board and to the Court of Federal Claims, and my signature (RFO FAR 33.205-6). It states that it is the contracting officer's final decision.

What I do not do: sit on it. Failure to issue a decision within the required period is a deemed denial, the contractor appeals anyway, and interest has been running the whole time. What I also do not do is issue a decision without legal review, or decide a claim involving fraud - those go to the appropriate investigative channel, not to me.

sections.heading: Interest
sections.body:
Yes, the Government pays interest. Under 41 U.S.C. 7109 and RFO FAR 33.205-3 (formerly 33.208), interest runs on a contractor's claim from the date the contracting officer receives a proper claim - certified if certification is required - or from the date payment would otherwise be due if that is later, until the date of payment.

The rate is set and published by the Secretary of the Treasury every six months for CDA purposes. It is simple interest, and it keeps running through my decision period, through an ASBCA appeal, and through litigation at the Court of Federal Claims. The Prompt Payment rate published for 1 July to 31 December 2026 in regulations.json is 4.75 percent per year; confirm the current semiannual rate before you quote a number.

Three things to keep straight. CDA interest is not Prompt Payment Act interest, which is about late payment of undisputed proper invoices (RFO FAR 32.907; 31 U.S.C. 3901). Interest runs in the other direction too - the contractor owes interest on a contract debt from the date of my demand letter (RFO FAR 32.608; FAR 52.232-17). And delay is expensive: every week I take to decide is a week of interest.

sections.heading: Appeals: ASBCA or the Court of Federal Claims
sections.body:
After my final decision the contractor elects one road and cannot take both.

- Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals: notice of appeal within 90 days of receipt of the decision (41 U.S.C. 7104(a)). Administrative judges, less formal, generally cheaper. The board offers a small-claims expedited procedure for claims of $50,000 or less, or $150,000 or less for a small business, and an accelerated procedure for claims of $100,000 or less - my decision letter has to tell the contractor these rights exist.
- U.S. Court of Federal Claims: a direct action within 12 months of receipt of the decision (41 U.S.C. 7104(b)). A judge, full litigation, appealable to the Federal Circuit.

The contractor may also use alternative dispute resolution at any point (RFO FAR 33.205-8) - and I should offer it. Q0129's short answer names the whole toolbox: ADR, an REA, a claim under the Disputes clause, the ASBCA, the Court of Federal Claims.

Throughout, performance continues. Under the Disputes clause the contractor must proceed diligently with performance pending final resolution of any request for relief.

key_cites.note: Disputes and Appeals, sections 33.205-1 through 33.205-9. The Part 33 deviation guide confirms the subpart and the 33.205-x series; the legacy numbers were 33.201 through 33.215.
Certification of claims over $100,000 (legacy 33.207). Threshold verified in regulations.json thresholds entry cda_claim_certification.
Interest on claims, formerly 33.208. Crosswalk confidence: verified.
Contracting officer's final decision: 60-day rule, required content, notice of the contractor's board and court election rights.
Alternative dispute resolution; available before or after the final decision.
Disputes clause: definition of claim, certification language at (d), duty to proceed diligently with performance pending resolution.

Contract Disputes Act. 7103(a)(4) six-year submission limit; 7103(b) certification and the curable-defect rule; 7104 appeal elections; 7106 expedited and accelerated board procedures; 7109 interest. Statute - unchanged by the RFO.
Prompt Payment interest penalties - a different animal from CDA interest. Standard payment period 30 days after a proper invoice; rate 4.75 percent for 1 Jul - 31 Dec 2026 per regulations.json.

board_angles.q: What makes a submission a claim?
board_angles.a: A written demand or assertion by a party, as a matter of right, for a sum certain or for adjustment or interpretation of contract terms - and over $100,000 it is not a claim until it is certified.

board_angles.q: Is a routine invoice a claim?
board_angles.a: No, not when it is submitted undisputed; it converts to a claim by written notice if it becomes disputed as to liability or amount, or if it is not acted on in a reasonable time.

board_angles.q: How long do you have to issue a final decision?
board_angles.a: Sixty days for a claim of $100,000 or less; for a larger claim, within 60 days I either decide or notify the contractor of a firm, reasonable date when I will, and failure to act is a deemed denial.

board_angles.q: Does the Government pay interest on claims?
board_angles.a: Yes - CDA interest at the Treasury rate from the date I receive a proper claim, or the date payment would otherwise be due if later, until payment, and it keeps running through my decision, the appeal and any litigation.

board_angles.q: Where does the contractor go after your final decision?
board_angles.a: Either the ASBCA within 90 days or the Court of Federal Claims within 12 months of receipt - the contractor elects one road, and my decision letter has to tell them both exist.

board_angles.q: What is the difference between an REA and a claim, and why do you care?
board_angles.a: An REA is a negotiable business proposal under a contract clause; a claim is a legal demand that starts certification, interest, my 60-day decision duty and appeal rights - so I try hard to settle at the REA stage.

The RFO section numbers 33.205-2, -3, -6 and -8 are verified in the crosswalk and used in the bank's own answers. Lower confidence on two points not fetched fresh: the exact RFO section that carries the definition of claim (the crosswalk confirms the 33.205-1 through -9 series but not which subsection holds the definitions - the rubric probe set uses 33.205-1), and the current Treasury CDA interest rate, which changes every six months.

title: Government Property: GFP, CAP and Who Eats the Loss
summary: Government property is anything the Government owns or acquires under a contract - property it furnishes to the contractor, and property the contractor buys with Government money. The default rule is that the Government self-insures and the contractor is not liable for loss, with a short list of exceptions that shift the risk. Furnishing property is a business decision that must be made before the solicitation goes out, not an afterthought a customer adds at kickoff.

sections.heading: Two kinds of property, one clause
sections.body:
Government-furnished property is property in the possession of, or acquired by, the Government and later furnished to the contractor. Contractor-acquired property is property the contractor buys or fabricates for performance and for which the Government has title or will take title under the contract.

Both are Government property, and both are managed under RFO FAR Part 45 with the basic clause FAR 52.245-1, Government Property. The clause obligates the contractor to have a property management system covering acquisition, receipt, records, physical inventory, subcontractor control, reports, relief of stewardship responsibility, utilization, maintenance, property closeout and disposition.

Government-furnished property also includes contractor-acquired property when that CAP is a deliverable under a cost contract and the Government accepts it for continued use under the contract.

Title depends on contract type and on what the contract says. Under cost-reimbursement and time-and-materials contracts the Government generally takes title to CAP when the cost is charged. Under fixed-price contracts, absent contract financing that vests title, the contractor typically holds title until delivery and acceptance - so read the contract before answering, as Q0161 does.

sections.heading: The decision to furnish, and getting it into the solicitation
sections.body:
Yes, a customer can have GFP - but the policy preference is that contractors furnish what they need to perform. Providing Government property is an exception that must be justified. Part 45 requires the Government to furnish property only when doing so is in the Government's best interest, and the decision drives evaluation, price and risk.

What has to happen before the solicitation goes out:

- The requiring activity identifies each item, its condition, quantity, location, and the date it will be available.
- The contracting officer confirms the property is available and serviceable - a promise of a forklift that is deadlined is a change order waiting to happen.
- The property is listed in the solicitation and in the contract, with a GFP attachment, so every offeror prices the same thing.
- The right clauses go in: FAR 52.245-1 with the appropriate alternate, plus the DFARS 252.245-70xx series.
- Property administration is assigned, and the COR's surveillance duties include it.

If the customer wants to add property after award, that is a change - price it, mod it, update the attachment.

sections.heading: Liability for loss: the default and the four exceptions
sections.body:
This is the single most-asked property question and the answer is counterintuitive to most customers. Under FAR 52.245-1(h), unless the contract provides otherwise, the contractor is not liable for loss of Government property furnished or acquired under the contract. The Government assumes the risk - it self-insures (RFO FAR 45.104).

The contractor is liable when any one of these applies:

- The risk is covered by insurance or the contractor is otherwise reimbursed.
- The loss results from willful misconduct or lack of good faith on the part of the contractor's managerial personnel.
- The contracting officer has, in writing, revoked the Government's assumption of risk because of a determination that the contractor's property management practices are inadequate, increase the Government's risk, or fail to provide adequate stewardship.
- The contract expressly makes the contractor liable - for example some fixed-price contracts, or where the contract specifies liability for particular items.

So the answer to "who pays to repair the GFP generator" is: normally the Government, unless one of those applies. And note the lever in the third exception - the revocation is mine, it is in writing, and it is prospective.

sections.heading: Property administration, reporting and disposal
sections.body:
The contracting officer is accountable, but the work is shared. A property administrator - often at DCMA under a contract administration delegation - conducts property management system analysis, approves or disapproves the contractor's system, and processes reports of loss. The COR does day-to-day surveillance and is usually the first to notice something wrong, as in the Q0161 fact pattern where the contractor is buying CAP and claiming it is theirs.

The contractor reports loss of Government property to the property administrator and the contracting officer. Relief of stewardship responsibility does not automatically mean relief of financial liability - those are two determinations.

When property is no longer needed, RFO FAR Subpart 45.6 governs reporting, reutilization and disposal: screening for reutilization within DoD, then transfer, donation, sale or abandonment, generally through the plant clearance process. At closeout, property disposition is one of the closeout steps - an open property account is a common reason a file cannot close.

Overseas adds layers. Property on an installation in Korea brings customs, import and SOFA questions; confirm the local procedure with C&P rather than assuming CONUS practice applies.

sections.heading: Traps and how boards probe it
sections.body:
The traps:

- Assuming the contractor pays for damage. The default is the opposite, and a candidate who gets this backwards looks like they have never administered a property contract.
- Letting a customer add GFP by e-mail after award. That is a change under the Changes clause and may be an unauthorized commitment if someone else promised it.
- Confusing title with possession, and answering the CAP question without asking what contract type it is.
- Forgetting that the clause has to be in the contract. No 52.245-1, no property management system requirement, and a much harder conversation later.
- Ignoring property at closeout.

How boards probe: they give you a lost or damaged item and ask who pays, then they add a fact - the contractor's property system was disapproved last quarter, or the loss happened because the site supervisor ignored a written warning - to see whether you can find the exception. Another common probe is the customer who wants to furnish property to "save money on the bid": the right answer is that it can, but only if it is identified, available, priced into the solicitation and administered, and that it transfers risk to the Government.

key_cites.note: Government Property. Part retained: 45.101-45.107 including 45.104 Responsibility and liability; Subpart 45.2 Solicitation and evaluation; 45.3 Use and rental; 45.4 Title; 45.6 Reporting, reutilization and disposal.
Responsibility and liability for Government property - the Government's assumption of risk and the conditions under which the contractor becomes liable.
Government Property clause, retained under the RFO and still prescribed by Part 45. Defines GFP and CAP, the property management system outcomes, reporting and disposition.

Contractor liability for Government property: not liable unless insured or reimbursed, willful misconduct or lack of good faith by managerial personnel, the contracting officer has revoked the assumption of risk in writing, or the contract provides otherwise.

key_cites.ref: DFARS Part 245 and the 252.245-70xx clause series
key_cites.note: DoD supplement for Government property, including reporting of Government property in the accountable property system of record. Confirm the current RFO DFARS deviation numbering before the board.

board_angles.q: Who is responsible for the cost of repair of Government-furnished property?
board_angles.a: Normally the Government - under 52.245-1(h) the contractor is not liable for loss of Government property unless the risk is insured or reimbursed, the loss came from willful misconduct or bad faith by managerial personnel, I have revoked the assumption of risk in writing, or the contract says otherwise.

board_angles.q: Your customer wants GFP in the solicitation. Can they do that, and what has to happen?
board_angles.a: Yes, if it is in the Government's best interest - but it has to be identified item by item with condition, quantity and availability, listed in the solicitation so every offeror prices the same thing, covered by 52.245-1 and the DoD clauses, and assigned to a property administrator.

board_angles.q: The COR reports the contractor is buying property under the contract and calling it their own. What do you do?
board_angles.a: I read the contract first - title to contractor-acquired property turns on contract type and the contract terms; under cost-type contracts the Government generally takes title as cost is charged, and if the contract vests title in the Government I correct the record and check the property management system.

board_angles.q: When would you revoke the Government's assumption of risk?
board_angles.a: When I determine in writing that the contractor's property management practices are inadequate, increase the Government's risk or fail to provide adequate stewardship - it is a written, prospective contracting officer action, usually after a disapproved property system.

board_angles.q: What happens to Government property at the end of the contract?
board_angles.a: Disposition under Subpart 45.6 - inventory, report, screen for reutilization, then transfer, donate, sell or abandon through plant clearance - and the property account has to be closed before the contract file can close.

Title rules under fixed-price versus cost contracts are stated as the bank's official Q0161 answer states them.

title: Closeout, CPARS and Contract Reporting
summary: The last twenty percent of a contract is where money gets left on the table and where the record either defends me or does not. Closeout deobligates funds and releases withholdings, contract action reports make the Government's spending visible, CPARS turns performance into something the next contracting officer can rely on, and the VCE Paperless Contract File is where all of it has to actually live. None of it is optional and all of it is graded.

sections.heading: The file: one place, complete, contemporaneous
sections.body:
The RFO collapsed old Subpart 4.8 into a single section. RFO FAR 4.101 requires each contracting, administration or paying office to establish a file for each solicitation and contractual action that comprehensively records the transaction history. The purposes stated in the rule are the ones to say aloud: background for the decisions made, support for the actions taken, information for reviews and investigations, and the facts if there is litigation or a congressional inquiry.

Note what changed. The old 4.803 itemized contents checklist is no longer regulatory. That is not a license to document less - it means the standard is now the outcome, not the checklist, and the burden of proving the file is complete moved to me.

Q0109 gives the practical framing: document so that anyone who picks up the file knows exactly where it stands, so the action complies with law and regulation, so I can defend the decision later, and so the Army's interests can be protected in litigation. Contract retention is Subpart 4.7; contractor record retention is generally three years after final payment (4.703), with category-specific periods at 4.705.

sections.heading: Closeout: why it matters and what it takes
sections.body:
Closeout is at RFO FAR 4.308, with 4.308-1 procedures and 4.308-2 closeout by the administering office. Why it matters, in the words of Q0007: excess funds may need to be deobligated, and many contract types withhold final payments that can be large sums to the contractor - a real cash-flow issue for a small business.

The timeframes carried on the RFO Part 4 deviation guide: six months for firm-fixed-price contracts and thirty-six months for contracts requiring settlement of indirect cost rates. The legacy rule also allowed twenty months for other contracts; confirm the current figure before you quote it.

The physically-complete-to-closed checklist: all deliverables accepted and the receiving report in place; final invoice and final payment; final indirect cost rate settlement where applicable; subcontract settlements; Government property disposed of and the property account closed; classified material dispositioned; patent and royalty reports; final CPARS entered; any claim or termination settled; contractor's release of claims; excess funds deobligated; and the file annotated and closed in the system of record.

Quick-closeout procedures for smaller unsettled indirect cost amounts sit in the indirect cost rate subpart (RFO Subpart 42.5, legacy 42.708) - confirm the section.

sections.heading: Contract action reporting after FPDS moved to SAM.gov
sections.body:
RFO FAR 4.301 requires agencies to report contract actions above the micro-purchase threshold to the Federal Procurement Data System, generally within three business days after award. What changed is the front door, not the duty: FPDS.gov was decommissioned in February 2026 and contract award data now lives in SAM.gov, which carries the contract data and the public search and reporting that FPDS.gov used to host. Verify the current entry point and any local workflow with C&P before the board - this transition is recent and the study decks still say FPDS-NG.

Why accuracy matters, per Q0048: the data is the basis for reports to the President, the Congress, GAO, federal agencies and the public; it measures the effect of federal contracting on the economy; and it is how small business, service-disabled veteran-owned, HUBZone, women-owned and other socioeconomic achievement is counted. A wrong NAICS code, set-aside code or dollar value misstates somebody's goal attainment and can distort a set-aside decision on the next requirement.

So I verify the CAR against the contract before it is finalized and fix errors by correcting the record, not by a workaround.

sections.heading: CPARS: writing a record somebody else will rely on
sections.body:
Contractor performance information is RFO FAR Subpart 42.11 (legacy 42.15), with 42.1100 scope, 42.1101 general, 42.1102 policy, 42.1103 procedures and 42.1104 the contract clause. Evaluations are required above dollar thresholds that vary by acquisition type; the legacy FAR 42.1502 figures were $1 million for services and IT, $5 million for systems and operations support, $750,000 for construction and $35,000 for architect-engineer work. Confirm the current RFO values before quoting them.

As assessing official, Q0124 tells you what to look for: complete and correct contract data - interim or final, contiguous periods of performance, program title and description; a meaningful narrative for every assessed area; specific events cited for any rating other than Satisfactory; a small business narrative addressing subcontracting goals and eSRS reporting; and assessments that are objective and verifiable rather than opinion.

Why it matters: other contracting officers evaluate past performance from these records, and an inflated rating on a poor performer is how a bad contractor keeps winning. The contractor gets to comment, so write something that survives a rebuttal.

sections.heading: VCE PCF discipline
sections.body:
The Virtual Contracting Enterprise Paperless Contract File is the Army's system of record for the contract file. If the document is not in the PCF, for practical purposes it does not exist: reviewers, auditors, the IG, a successor contracting officer and Army legal all work from the PCF.

What I do personally, not by delegation:

- Build the file as I go rather than at closeout. A file assembled from memory six months later is a file with holes.
- Check that documents in the PCF are the signed, final versions and that the metadata - contract number, modification number, dates, dollar values - matches the contract and the contract action report.
- Spot-check my specialists' files at award and at each modification.
- Reconcile the PCF against the CAR and CPARS entries; three systems telling three stories is an audit finding.
- Close out PCF actions before a departure. In VCE-Warrants a departing member's PCF actions must be zero before removal from the TDA is enabled.

Confirm the current 411th PCF review procedures and any local checklist with C&P.

key_cites.note: Contract files. Old 4.801, 4.802 and 4.803 collapsed into one section; the itemized contents checklist is no longer regulatory.
Contract reporting: report actions above the micro-purchase threshold to FPDS within three business days after award. Fetched from the Part 4 deviation guide 14 Sep 2026.
Contract closeout; 4.308-1 procedures, 4.308-2 closeout by the administering office with six months for firm-fixed-price and thirty-six months for indirect cost rate settlement.
Contractor records retention: generally three years after final payment (4.703), with category-specific periods at 4.705.
Contractor performance information, formerly Subpart 42.15. Sections 42.1100 scope, 42.1101 general, 42.1102 policy, 42.1103 procedures, 42.1104 contract clause.
Assignment of contract administration - how functions are delegated to a contract administration office such as DCMA, which matters for who actually closes the file.
FPDS.gov was decommissioned in February 2026 and federal contract award data moved to SAM.gov. Verify the current reporting entry point and local workflow with C&P; the FAR text still names FPDS.

board_angles.q: Why is contract closeout important?
board_angles.a: Because excess funds have to be deobligated and put back to work, withheld final payments are released to the contractor, and an open file keeps property, indirect rates and subcontract settlements unresolved - it is the last chance to get the record right.

board_angles.q: What are the closeout timeframes?
board_angles.a: Under RFO FAR 4.308-2, six months after the file is physically complete for firm-fixed-price contracts and thirty-six months where indirect cost rates have to be settled; I would confirm the intermediate figure for other contract types.

board_angles.q: Why must contract action reports be complete and accurate?
board_angles.a: The data feeds reports to the President, Congress, GAO and the public, measures the effect of federal contracting on the economy, and is how socioeconomic goal achievement is counted - a wrong code misstates somebody's numbers and can distort the next set-aside decision.

board_angles.q: You are the assessing official on a CPARS evaluation. What are you looking for?
board_angles.a: Complete and correct contract data, a meaningful narrative for every area, specific events cited for any rating other than Satisfactory, a small business narrative that addresses goals and eSRS, and assessments that are objective and verifiable - because other contracting officers will make source selection decisions from it.

board_angles.q: What is the VCE PCF and how do you personally ensure the data is accurate?
board_angles.a: It is the Army's paperless contract file, the system of record - so I build the file as I go, verify signed final versions and matching metadata, reconcile the PCF against the contract action report and CPARS, and spot-check my specialists' files at award and at each modification.

board_angles.q: Why document the file at all?
