title: Grants, Cooperative Agreements and Other Transactions
summary: Not everything the Government funds is a contract. When the principal purpose is to transfer a thing of value to carry out a public purpose, the law requires an assistance instrument - a grant or a cooperative agreement - and when the Government needs a prototype from companies that will not take a FAR contract, an Other Transaction may be the right tool. Different instrument, different rulebook, different warrant: Grants Officer, Agreements Officer and Contracting Officer are three separate appointments.

sections.heading: Choosing the instrument: the principal purpose test
sections.body:
Congress settled this in 31 U.S.C. 6303-6305, and it is a purpose test, not a preference test.

- Procurement contract, 31 U.S.C. 6303: the principal purpose is to acquire property or services for the direct benefit or use of the Federal Government. Agencies have inherent constitutional authority to contract.
- Grant, 31 U.S.C. 6304: the principal purpose is to transfer a thing of value to a recipient to carry out a public purpose of support or stimulation authorized by law, and substantial involvement between the agency and the recipient is not expected.
- Cooperative agreement, 31 U.S.C. 6305: same public purpose, but substantial involvement is expected between the agency and the recipient in carrying out the activity.

Substantial involvement is the hinge between the last two - collaborative participation in the work, agency approval of stages or personnel, direction of the effort. Attending meetings and reading reports is not substantial involvement.

One more rule boards love: unlike contracting, an assistance instrument requires authorizing legislation. So a program office that wants a grant because it is faster gets a purpose test and an authority question, not a form.

sections.heading: The rulebook and its order of precedence
sections.body:
For DoD assistance the stack is:

- Federal statute and law.
- Government-wide regulation, executive orders and OMB guidance - principally 2 CFR Part 200, the uniform administrative requirements, cost principles and audit requirements for federal awards.
- Agency regulation: the DoD Grants and Agreements Regulations, the DoDGARs, at 32 CFR Chapter I Subchapter C - Part 21 general, Part 22 grants and cooperative agreements, Part 28 drug-free workplace and lobbying, Part 34 administrative requirements for for-profit recipients, Part 37 technology investment agreements - plus the DoD implementation of 2 CFR 200 in the 2 CFR Part 1100 series. The Grants Officer is defined in 2 CFR 1108.
- Standard terms and conditions, then award-specific terms and conditions, then agency policy.

The point to make out loud is the ordering principle: law trumps everything, then government-wide regulation, then agency regulation, then the award's own terms. Different sources present this list slightly differently, so state the principle and offer to confirm the exact sequence.

Assistance awards are reported to the Defense Assistance Award Data System, DAADS, under DoDGARs Part 21.535, and announcements of funding opportunities go out electronically through Grants.gov.

sections.heading: Running an assistance award
sections.body:
The Grants Officer's core responsibilities are compact: ensure awards are used effectively in executing DoD programs and are made and administered in accordance with law, executive orders, regulation and DoD policy; ensure sufficient funds are available for obligation; and ensure recipients receive impartial, fair and equitable treatment.

The life cycle: announce the opportunity electronically; conduct merit review; determine recipient qualification and run the risk review under 2 CFR 200 - financial stability, quality of management systems, history of performance, audit findings, ability to meet the requirements; determine allowability under the applicable cost principles; make the award with standard and special terms; monitor performance and reporting; handle noncompliance with the remedies ladder up to suspension and termination; audit; and close out.

Audits of a state or local government recipient come through the Single Audit process under 2 CFR 200 Subpart F, not by sending an auditor - the Grants Officer obtains and reviews the Single Audit report and follows up findings.

Competition: there is no CICA for assistance, but merit-based competitive procedures are the policy expectation, and a Grants Officer should seek competition. Fiscal law does not relax because the instrument is a grant.

sections.heading: Other Transactions: authority, conditions and limits
sections.body:
An Other Transaction is not a procurement contract, not a grant, not a cooperative agreement and not a CRADA. It is a binding instrument used where the FAR-based system would keep the right performers out.

Authorities: 10 U.S.C. 4021 for research OTs (formerly 2371) and 4022 for prototype projects (formerly 2371b), with follow-on production at 4022(f).

A prototype OT under 4022 requires a project directly relevant to enhancing the mission effectiveness of military personnel and the supporting platforms, systems, components or materials, or improving those in use by the armed forces - plus one condition: a nontraditional defense contractor participating to a significant extent; all significant participants nontraditional or small business; at least one-third of total cost from non-federal sources; or a senior procurement executive determination that exceptional circumstances justify innovative business arrangements not feasible under a contract.

A nontraditional defense contractor has not performed, for at least one year before the solicitation, a DoD contract or subcontract subject to full CAS coverage.

What does not apply: CICA, TINA, the Contract Disputes Act, the protest system, Bayh-Dole, the DoDGARs. What does apply: criminal law, fiscal law in full, Comptroller General access to records, security and OPSEC, export control.

sections.heading: Follow-on production and the numbers
sections.body:
The most probed OT rule is the follow-on. Under 10 U.S.C. 4022(f) a follow-on production contract or transaction may go to the participants without further competition only if competitive procedures were used to select the parties for the transaction and the participants successfully completed the prototype project. Say both, in that order - candidates routinely give only the second.

Approval thresholds are where the bank is inconsistent. Q0184 gives up to $50 million to the SCO, $50-100 million the HCA, $100-500 million the SPE, above $500 million OSD. Q0192 gives up to $50 million SCO, $50-250 million SPE, over $250 million USD. Both are official. Do not pick one - say the level scales by dollar value from SCO through HCA, the Army SPE and OSD, name the $50 million SCO tier they agree on, and confirm the current table. A separate D&F is executed for each prototype project.

Warrants: the Grants Officer is appointed by the HCA, not delegable. Agreements Officer warrants are delegable to the SCO and no lower than the chief of the contracting office; Policy v12 wants CON 0660 and Neg-OTA-tion 101 or equivalent, a commensurate KO or GO warrant, and working knowledge of data rights.

key_cites.note: The principal purpose test: 6303 procurement contract, 6304 grant, 6305 cooperative agreement with substantial involvement. Statute, unchanged by the RFO; 6304 and 6305 are on the regulations.json unchanged list.

Uniform administrative requirements, cost principles and audit requirements for federal awards, including the recipient risk review and the Subpart F Single Audit. On the regulations.json unchanged list. DoD implementation is the 2 CFR 1100 series; Grants Officer is defined at 2 CFR 1108.

key_cites.note: Parts 21 general (including 21.535 DAADS reporting), 22 grants and cooperative agreements, 28 drug-free workplace and lobbying, 34 for-profit recipients, 37 technology investment agreements. Agreements Officer is defined at 32 CFR 3.4.
Research projects: transactions other than contracts and grants. Renumbered from 10 U.S.C. 2371 by Pub. L. 116-283, effective 1 Jan 2022. Crosswalk confidence: verified.

DoD authority for prototype projects, renumbered from 2371b. Subsection (f) governs follow-on production: competitive procedures used to select participants, and successful completion of the prototype project. Some sources in the bank call this 4003b; no such section exists.

Hosted on the PAM Army Warranting Program page (CAC).

board_angles.q: A program office wants a grant so they do not have to compete. What do you tell them?
board_angles.a: The instrument is decided by the principal purpose test, not by convenience - if the purpose is to acquire property or services for the Government's direct benefit it is a contract under 31 U.S.C. 6303, and an assistance award also requires authorizing legislation, which a contract does not.

board_angles.q: What is the difference between a grant and a cooperative agreement?
board_angles.a: Both transfer a thing of value to carry out a public purpose; the difference is substantial involvement - expected in a cooperative agreement under 31 U.S.C. 6305, not expected in a grant under 6304.

board_angles.q: What is the authority for a prototype Other Transaction, and what conditions must be met?
board_angles.a: 10 U.S.C. 4022 - a prototype project directly relevant to mission effectiveness, plus one of the four conditions: a nontraditional participating significantly, all significant participants nontraditional or small business, at least one-third non-federal cost share, or an SPE determination of exceptional circumstances.

board_angles.q: When can a follow-on production award go to the OT participants without competition?
board_angles.a: Under 10 U.S.C. 4022(f), only if competitive procedures were used to select the parties for the prototype transaction and the participants successfully completed the prototype project.

board_angles.q: What does not apply to an OT, and what still does?
board_angles.a: CICA, TINA, the Contract Disputes Act, the protest system, Bayh-Dole and the DoDGARs do not apply; criminal law, federal fiscal law, Comptroller General access to records, security and OPSEC, export control and DoDI 5000 programmatic requirements still do.

board_angles.q: Can a Grants Officer sign an Other Transaction?
board_angles.a: No - an OT is not a grant or cooperative agreement, and it takes an Agreements Officer warrant with its own qualifications; a person may hold KO, GO and AO warrants, but each is a separate appointment with separate requirements.

title: Korea for Contracting Officers: LCS and SOFA
summary: Two things make contracting in the Republic of Korea different from anywhere else an Army contracting officer works: Logistics Cost Sharing money, which the Republic of Korea holds and spends on behalf of United States Forces Korea, and the Status of Forces Agreement, which decides whether a U.S. contractor can even perform here. On an LCS action the 411th contracting officer recommends; the Republic of Korea Ministry of National Defense approves, awards and pays. Everything in this primer is drawn from 411th study-group sources and must be confirmed with C&P before you rely on it at a board or on a file.

sections.heading: The Special Measures Agreement and what LCS is
sections.body:
The Special Measures Agreement is the defense cost-sharing arrangement between the United States and the Republic of Korea under which the ROK provides financial support for the costs of stationing United States Forces Korea on the peninsula.

The Logistics Cost Sharing program is one portion of the SMA. It partially offsets the logistical costs of USFK operations - things like movement of personnel and assets, repair and maintenance services, and the purchase of non-tactical vehicles.

The critical structural fact: LCS funds are never transferred to the United States. They are held by the ROK Ministry of National Defense, which uses them to purchase goods and services for USFK. That single sentence explains every downstream oddity - who awards, who pays, who competes, and why the timeline is longer.

Because it is ROK money spent under ROK rules for a shared purpose, an LCS action is not an ordinary Army procurement that happens to be overseas. A candidate who treats it as one will get the whole scenario wrong, and the 411th board will ask.

sections.heading: Who does what on an LCS action
sections.body:
The lanes, as the 411th study-group sources describe them:

- USFK J4 manages the LCS program. Packages route through J4.
- The 411th CSB provides the contract vehicles and runs the procurement work - requirement development with the customer, solicitation, evaluation.
- The 411th contracting officer makes a recommendation for award through USFK J4. The 411th KO does not award LCS contracts.
- ROK MND approves and awards the LCS contract.
- Invoices are submitted to ROK MND and payments are made by ROK MND.

Say the boundary out loud at a board, because the whole question is whether you know the limit of your own signature: on an LCS requirement my authority is to run a sound procurement and recommend; the award decision and the money are the ROK's.

The practical consequence is time. ROK MND approval adds a step no O&M action has. On an $11 million grounds maintenance requirement like Q0276, I plan backward from the customer's need date with the MND window built in, tell the customer that date early and in writing, and do not promise an award date I do not control.

sections.heading: Restrictions and the O&M separation
sections.body:
Limitations on LCS, from the 411th sources:

- The program is limited to local Korean businesses; Korean material and Korean labor must be used.
- LCS contracts require additional time for ROK MND approval.
- As of January 2022 ROK MND no longer requires an approved offshore waiver before submission; instead a memo documenting whether offshore or local materials are used must be submitted with all LCS packages to J4. Confirm the current form and routing with C&P - this one has already changed once.

The rule that shows up most often: O&M and LCS funds cannot be combined in a single solicitation. The reason is a competition conflict, not an accounting preference. A U.S. O&M requirement must generally be solicited using full and open competitive procedures unless a FAR exception applies; an LCS requirement must be solicited under procedures limited to Korean contractors. One solicitation cannot carry contradictory competition requirements. So when the customer asks to bundle the two to save time, the answer is no, the explanation is competition, and the lawful path is two separate actions.

At an $11 million estimate, note the ordinary consequences: simplified procedures are unavailable and a source selection plan is required.

sections.heading: SOFA Article XV and the Invited Contractor program
sections.body:
All U.S. contractors supporting USFK contracts are required to obtain SOFA designation through the FKAQ Invited Contractor program. Article XV of the SOFA and USFK Instruction 4901.01 carry the requirements.

It is a two-step process and the split matters:

- Step one is mine. The contracting officer submits a request for contract SOFA designation to USFK/FKAQ, after reviewing Article XV and USFKI 4901.01 for requirements unique to performance in the ROK.
- Step two belongs to the requiring activity. The RA obtains SOFA designation for the individual contractor employees.

The 411th source describes four unique requirements a U.S. contractor must meet to perform in the ROK, beginning with security considerations. Get the current list from C&P and FKAQ rather than reciting a guess - a wrong list is worse than saying you would confirm it.

What IC status affects in practice: entry and residence status, access to installations and to the logistics support system, customs handling, and taxation treatment. None of it is mine to grant - I request it, FKAQ designates it. Build the lead time into the acquisition schedule and put the contractor's SOFA obligations into the contract.

sections.heading: Exercise and contingency support, and how boards probe Korea
sections.body:
Korea runs on exercises. Requirements arrive with fixed, externally driven dates, and the pressure to shortcut is real. Two guardrails: an exercise is foreseeable, so a late requirement is a planning failure, not an urgency justification - unusual and compelling urgency under Part 6 is narrow, documented, and costly to the customer later. And contingency dollar thresholds do not apply just because something feels urgent; the higher micro-purchase and simplified acquisition figures attach to a designated contingency, humanitarian or emergency operation. The OCONUS contingency values in regulations.json are $40,000 and $2,000,000. Confirm a designation is actually in effect before using them.

How the board probes Korea: they hand you an LCS scenario and watch whether you claim the award, ask to combine funding sources and watch for the competition explanation, and ask the two-step SOFA question to see which step you think is yours. A 411th board must include at least one Korea item, so this is not optional study.

Safe closing sentence on any Korea answer: name the rule from the source, then say you would confirm the current procedure with C&P and, for LCS, USFK J4.

key_cites.note: LCS is a portion of the SMA; ROK MND holds the funds, USFK J4 manages the program, 411th KOs recommend award, ROK MND approves, awards and pays. From 411th study-group sources; confirm with C&P and USFK J4.
Invited Contractor status for U.S. contractors performing in the ROK. Designation is obtained through USFK/FKAQ.

Implements the Invited Contractor program: the two-step process, the contracting officer's request for contract SOFA designation and the requiring activity's request for individual designation, and the unique requirements for performance in the ROK.

Micro-purchase threshold $40,000 and simplified acquisition threshold $2,000,000 outside the United States for a contingency, CBRN defense, disaster or emergency operation; 41 U.S.C. 1903. Values from regulations.json thresholds, status 'verify'.
Unusual and compelling urgency and the justification and approval tiers - relevant when an exercise requirement arrives late. Lack of advance planning is not a justification.

board_angles.q: What is the Logistics Cost Sharing program?
board_angles.a: It is the portion of the U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement that partially offsets USFK logistical costs - movement of personnel and assets, repair and maintenance, non-tactical vehicles - with funds the ROK holds rather than transfers to the United States.

board_angles.q: An $11 million LCS grounds maintenance requirement lands on your desk. Who awards it?
board_angles.a: Not me. The 411th runs the procurement and I make a recommendation for award through USFK J4; ROK MND approves and awards the contract and pays the invoices - and I build the MND approval window into the schedule I give the customer.

board_angles.q: Can you fund one contract with both O&M and LCS?
board_angles.a: No. O&M actions are solicited under full and open competition unless a FAR exception applies, and LCS actions are limited to Korean contractors - one solicitation cannot carry contradictory competition requirements, so it has to be two actions.

board_angles.q: What are the limitations of LCS funds?
board_angles.a: Korean businesses only, Korean labor and material, a longer timeline for ROK MND approval, and a memo documenting offshore or local materials with every package to J4 - and I would confirm the current package requirements with C&P.

board_angles.q: What is the Invited Contractor program and whose job is each step?
board_angles.a: It is the FKAQ program that gives U.S. contractors SOFA status under Article XV and USFKI 4901.01; step one, SOFA designation for the contract, is the contracting officer's, and step two, designation of the individual contractor employees, is the requiring activity's.

board_angles.q: The exercise starts in three weeks and the requirement just arrived. Does that justify a sole source?
board_angles.a: Not on its own - an exercise is foreseeable and lack of advance planning is not a justification; unusual and compelling urgency under RFO FAR 6.103-2 is narrow, has to be justified and approved at the right level, and limits what I can buy.

title: Ethics, Procurement Integrity and Conflicts of Interest
summary: A warrant is a trust, and the board is deciding whether to give you one. Procurement integrity law controls what you may do with proposal and source selection information and what happens when you talk to a company about a job; the organizational conflict of interest rules control whether a company can compete fairly at all; and the fraud and gratuities rules control what you do the moment something smells wrong. The through-line is the same in every one of them: disclose early, involve legal and the ethics counselor, document, and never decide alone.

sections.heading: Procurement integrity: the three prohibitions
sections.body:
RFO FAR 3.104 implements 41 U.S.C. chapter 21, and the section number survived the overhaul: 3.104-1 definitions through 3.104-9 clauses, with 3.104-3 prohibitions, 3.104-4 disclosure and protection of information, 3.104-5 disqualification and 3.104-7 violations.

The three things the statute forbids:

- Disclosing contractor bid or proposal information or source selection information before award to anyone not authorized to receive it. The Q0159 list: cost or pricing data, indirect cost and direct labor rates, proprietary manufacturing or operational information the contractor marked as protected by law, and anything marked contractor bid or proposal information.
- Obtaining such information improperly.
- Employment discussions. An official participating personally and substantially in a procurement over the simplified acquisition threshold who is contacted by a bidder about non-federal employment must report the contact in writing and either reject it or disqualify themselves (3.104-3 and 3.104-5).

If I learn of a possible violation, 3.104-7 governs: I do not investigate and I do not confront. I notify legal and my chief immediately, assess the impact on the pending award, and report through the chain to the head of the contracting activity, who decides whether award proceeds.

sections.heading: Organizational conflicts of interest: three types, four responses
sections.body:
An OCI exists when, because of other activities or relationships, a contractor is unable or potentially unable to render impartial assistance or advice, its objectivity in performing the work is or might be impaired, or it has an unfair competitive advantage (RFO FAR 9.501).

The three types:

- Unequal access to information. The contractor got nonpublic Government or third-party information through other work - the IGE, the draft work statement, the evaluation approach, a competitor's proprietary data (9.505-4).
- Biased ground rules. The contractor wrote the specification, the work statement or the evaluation criteria and then competes against them (9.505-2).
- Impaired objectivity. The contractor would evaluate, audit or advise on its own work or a competitor's.

The duty at 9.504 is to identify potential conflicts as early in the acquisition process as possible and to avoid, neutralize or mitigate them before award. The tools: restructure the requirement, exclude the contractor, firewall with real teeth, release the information to everyone, or a waiver - which only the agency head or designee grants under 9.503, not me.

Whatever the resolution, it goes into the solicitation as a term (9.507) and into the file with legal's concurrence.

sections.heading: Gifts, gratuities and post-Government employment
sections.body:
Personal ethics sits on top of the procurement rules, and the standards are stricter for contracting people because our signature moves money.

Gifts and gratuities. The Standards of Ethical Conduct and the Joint Ethics Regulation, DoD 5500.07-R, govern. The working rule: do not accept gifts, meals, entertainment or anything of value from a prohibited source - a current or prospective contractor - because the narrow exceptions are not worth the risk when you hold a warrant. The Gratuities clause lets the Government terminate for gratuities offered to obtain a contract or favorable treatment. When a vendor invites the team to dinner after award the answer is no, the team is told why on the spot, and if someone already went I report it rather than handling it quietly.

Post-Government employment. Three layers: the criminal statutes at 18 U.S.C. 207 - a lifetime ban on switching sides on a particular matter you worked personally and substantially, a two-year ban on matters under your official responsibility, a one-year cooling-off for senior officials; the procurement integrity one-year compensation ban at 41 U.S.C. 2104; and the employment-contact reporting rule above. Anyone approaching retirement or a job offer sees the ethics counselor first, in writing.

sections.heading: Fraud indicators and reporting
sections.body:
Indicators worth naming: bids with suspiciously similar language or identical errors; a rotation pattern in who wins; prices that jump when one bidder drops out; invoices for work the COR cannot confirm; a vendor pressing for a specific person on the evaluation team; changed or missing receiving reports; split purchases that hug a threshold; a requirement written around one product; a COR who resists giving surveillance documentation; relationships that are too comfortable.

What I do, and the order matters: do not investigate, do not confront the suspected party, preserve documents and electronic records, report the same day. Channels from Q0040: the Procurement Fraud Advisor under AFARS 5109.406-3; a flash report through legal under AR 27-40 chapter 8 and the Procurement Fraud Branch through the HCA; the DoD Inspector General hotline and Army CID; the ethics counselor for gratuities and conflicts; and for a procurement integrity violation the 3.104-7 route to the HCA. On legal advice I may hold suspicious invoices - but I do not stop payment on my own theory.

Mentoring the customer is part of the job: brief ethics and fraud at the post-award conference, meet the hotline poster requirement at RFO FAR 3.1003, and use real cases.

sections.heading: Saying no to leadership
sections.body:
This question is on nearly every board, and it is not a test of courage - it is a test of method.

The method: first, make sure you are right - get the legal parameters from counsel before you plant a flag. Second, understand their reasoning; ask what outcome leadership needs, because there is often a lawful way to get it. Third, take the legal position and the leadership position back to counsel together. Fourth, if a conflict remains, raise it to your supervisor and up the chain; you do not have to go it alone. Fifth, put it in writing - a memorandum to file or confirming e-mail recording the direction, the concern and the advice received. Sixth, offer the lawful alternative.

And the line. If it is still wrong, I do not sign. Management cannot make a contracting officer sign. The warrant is mine and so is the accountability. The bank's official answers say it plainly: never sign a contract you are not comfortable signing.

The related boundary is inherently governmental work: a contractor employee cannot be a voting member of a source selection board, no matter how unique the expertise or how senior the person asking (Q0133).

board_angles.q: What is an organizational conflict of interest and what do you do about one?
board_angles.a: It is when a contractor cannot be impartial, its objectivity is impaired, or it has an unfair competitive advantage - and under 9.504 I identify it as early as possible and avoid, neutralize or mitigate it before award, with legal, with the resolution written into the solicitation; only the agency head can waive it.

board_angles.q: Give me an example of unequal access to information.
board_angles.a: A program-office support contractor that saw the independent Government estimate, the draft performance work statement and the evaluation approach, then bids on the follow-on - I either release the information to everyone, firewall it, or exclude them.

board_angles.q: What proposal information may you not disclose?
board_angles.a: Cost or pricing data, indirect cost and direct labor rates, proprietary manufacturing or operational information the contractor marked as protected, and anything marked as contractor bid or proposal information - disclosure before award is a procurement integrity violation under 3.104.

board_angles.q: A company offers you a job during a source selection. What happens?
board_angles.a: I report the contact in writing and then either reject it outright or disqualify myself from the procurement, and I tell my chief and the ethics counselor - that is 3.104-3 and 3.104-5, and it is criminal law behind it, not etiquette.

board_angles.q: You suspect fraud on one of your contracts. What do you do?
board_angles.a: I do not investigate and I do not confront anyone. I preserve the documents and records, notify legal and my chief the same day, contact the Procurement Fraud Advisor, and let the flash report and IG or CID channels work - and I hold suspicious invoices only on legal advice.

board_angles.q: Leadership directs you to do something you believe is contrary to your legal guidance. What do you do?
board_angles.a: I confirm the legal position, ask what outcome they need, take both positions back to counsel, raise it through my chain, put the direction and my concern in writing, and offer the lawful alternative - and if it is still wrong I do not sign, because management cannot make a contracting officer sign.

title: The Army Warranting Program
summary: A warrant is an individual's signatory authority to enter into, obligate funds for, administer, terminate and sign documents under specific appointed or delegated authorities, for FAR-based and non-FAR-based instruments alike. The Army Warranting Program Policy, version 12 of March 2026, sets four warrant classes, a fixed threshold at each class, a rule for calculating the value an instrument counts against your warrant, and a review board that says whether you are ready. VCE-Warrants is the record for all of it.

sections.heading: Who appoints, and the three warrant types
sections.body:
The chain: ASA(ALT) designated procurement authority to DASA(P); DASA(P) may further delegate selection, appointment and termination of contracting officers under RFO FAR 1.403-1(b), and of Grants Officers and Agreements Officers under 32 CFR 21.425; DASA(P) delegates warrant-granting authority to the head of the contracting activity.

For KOs and AOs the HCA may delegate down to a Senior Contracting Official and no lower than the Chief of the Contracting Office; where delegated, 'HCA' in the policy means that delegated official. For Grants Officers the HCA appoints directly and shall not delegate further. At the 411th CSB the SCO chairs the board and makes the appointment in VCE-Warrants.

Three warrant types, three definitions: KO, defined in the FAR and used collectively for procuring, administrative, contingency and termination contracting officers; GO, defined in 2 CFR 1108; AO, defined in 32 CFR 3.4.

One person may hold more than one type, but must meet the qualifications for each. What HCAs may not do is issue the same type twice - a PCO and an ACO warrant to one person - merely to split pre-award and post-award dollar limits. A warrant genuinely limited to an administrative or termination function is still allowed.

sections.heading: Classes, thresholds and calculating instrument value
sections.body:
Policy v12 Table 1 sets four classes and fixed thresholds:

- Class I: SAT, currently $350,000.
- Class II: $500K, $1M, $5M and SaP - simplified procedures for commercial products and services, currently $9,000,000, or $15,000,000 for a contingency, CBRN defense, disaster or emergency operation.
- Class III: $10M, $25M, $50M and $100M.
- Class IV: $250M, $500M and Unlimited.

Warrants are granted at one of those fixed values. Appointing at 'SAT' or 'SaP' rather than a dollar figure means nobody has to be reappointed when the underlying value changes. The threshold applies to everything: FAR-based and non-FAR-based instruments, contracts, delivery and task orders, agreements and modifications.

The calculation rule from paragraph 4.2 is the one boards test. The warrant must be greater than or equal to the cumulative instrument value, and that equals base value plus all options plus any anticipated or actual ceiling plus the absolute value of a modification - regardless of when funds are obligated. Two consequences: a five-year requirement with a modest first year can exceed a Class II warrant on day one, and a deobligating modification still counts at its absolute value. Work the math before you accept the file, not at signature.

sections.heading: The boards: CORB, GORB and AORB
sections.body:
The review board is how the HCA verifies readiness and the strength of a candidate's decision making. There is one per warrant type - the Contracting Officer Review Board, the Grants Officer Review Board and the Agreements Officer Review Board.

Policy v12's general rule: the HCA, or the delegated official, chairs and administers the board and selects three to five additional members with a mix of experience, legal expertise and supervisory backgrounds appropriate to the warrant type. Questions must be commensurate with the warrant threshold, the candidate's role, the organization's mission, the instruments the candidate will sign, and the responsibility to be assumed.

At the 411th CSB, per the July 2026 warrant process workflow: the SCO chairs; voting members come from the SCO, PD, CoCO and/or Division Chiefs and KOs; CONOPS and the Chief, C&P facilitate and do not vote; the board sits the second Wednesday of each month. CONOPS and C&P prepare the questions, cover sheet and scoring sheet, generate the warrant number, and prepare the draft appointment memorandum and certificate for VCE-Warrants. The SCO appoints only on a unanimous recommendation. Confirm current procedures with C&P.

sections.heading: Waivers, legacy warrants and reciprocity
sections.body:
Waivers. The HCA may waive qualification requirements, including the review board, in writing, justified by a risk assessment of the individual's knowledge, skills and abilities with sound rationale and a business case. KO waivers must also comply with 10 U.S.C. 1724(d). Every waiver goes into VCE-Warrants before appointment. The hard limit: the board for an Unlimited warrant cannot be waived. At the 411th a CORB waiver rests on SCO approval, with the memoranda and certificate uploaded in VCE.

Legacy warrants. A person holding a current warrant is not required to be tested, re-boarded or reappointed to keep it, and the exemption extends to increases within the same Table 1 class. To move up a class, the individual takes a new board and is reappointed, completing any qualifications that changed.

Reciprocity. Under ACC Contracting Note 26-03, all ACC SCOs must honor all active and future warrants issued within ACC. Recognition is formal acceptance of an existing warrant's type and value by a different SCO - the individual acts under the recognizing SCO's authority and no new warrant is issued. Warrants from outside ACC are recognized at the SCO's discretion, and a new ACC warrant must still be issued in VCE.

sections.heading: VCE-Warrants: suspension, termination, reinstatement, transfer
sections.body:
VCE-Warrants is the system of record. Every appointment, waiver, suspension, termination and reinstatement is documented and retained there.

Suspension. Reasons in Policy v12 include extended temporary duty, a performance improvement plan, investigation of the holder's actions, and deployment or support to a contingency. It is also the mechanism for a developmental assignment to another organization - and must not be used in lieu of termination.

Termination. Mandatory when the individual leaves employment or moves to a non-acquisition position; also for a change in mission requirements, unsatisfactory performance or misconduct such as Antideficiency Act violations, fraud or negligence, loss of a required clearance, or exceeding delegated authority. Retroactive terminations are prohibited. At the 411th, C&P uploads the termination documents to the VCE record and then terminates; removal from the VCE TDA requires the member's PCF actions to be zero.

Reinstatement. The HCA may reinstate a suspended warrant; a terminated warrant requires a new Certificate of Appointment and letter. Transfer between HCA organizations is not supported by the system, so the original is terminated and a complete new record is built under the gaining SCO. Records are retained six years from suspension or termination unless a longer period is justified in writing.

sections.heading: Where the FAR overhaul stands (October 2026)
sections.body: Cite RFO numbering: the Army Warranting Program Policy v12 made the overhauled FAR, DFARS and AFARS effective in Army practice on 1 February 2026, through class deviations. The FAR Council is now writing the same text into the FAR itself: proposed rules for 20 parts were published on 23 June 2026 and a second batch (Parts 8, 9, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 27, 28, 35, 36, 38, 44, 47 and 51, with their Part 52 clauses) on 18 September 2026, each with a 30-day comment period. No final rule had been published by 29 October 2026, so the deviation text still governs. A board member who asks 'is the RFO final?' wants to hear exactly that: in effect by deviation, in formal rulemaking, not yet final. Check acquisition.gov/far-overhaul for the current state before your board.

board_angles.q: What are the four warrant classes and their thresholds?
board_angles.a: Class I at the SAT, currently $350,000; Class II at $500K, $1M, $5M and SaP, currently $9 million; Class III at $10M, $25M, $50M and $100M; Class IV at $250M, $500M and Unlimited.

board_angles.q: How do you calculate the value an instrument counts against your warrant?
board_angles.a: Cumulative instrument value - base plus all options plus any anticipated or actual ceiling plus the absolute value of a modification, regardless of when funds are obligated - and my warrant has to be greater than or equal to that number.

board_angles.q: Your $4M contract needs a modification that pushes cumulative value past your threshold. What do you do?
board_angles.a: I stop, because the threshold covers modifications at absolute value; I prepare the action completely and route it to a contracting officer whose warrant covers the cumulative value, and I tell the customer early rather than at signature.

board_angles.q: Can a warrant board be waived?
board_angles.a: Yes by the HCA in writing, on a documented risk assessment with sound rationale and a business case, with the waiver in VCE-Warrants before appointment and compliance with 10 U.S.C. 1724(d) for KOs - except the board for an Unlimited warrant, which cannot be waived.

board_angles.q: You PCS to another ACC organization. What happens to your warrant?
board_angles.a: Under ACC Contracting Note 26-03 all ACC SCOs must honor active ACC warrants; if I am working under a different SCO the warrant is recognized at its existing value with no new warrant, and on a permanent reassignment the old warrant is terminated and a complete new record is built under the gaining SCO because VCE does not transfer.

board_angles.q: When is a warrant suspended versus terminated?
board_angles.a: Suspension is temporary - extended TDY, a performance improvement plan, an investigation, a deployment, or a developmental assignment - and it must not be used in lieu of termination; termination is mandatory on leaving the position and applies for misconduct, loss of clearance or exceeding authority, and it can never be retroactive.

title: Board Day: How a CORB Works and How to Answer
summary: A warrant board is not a test of memory; it is a panel of people deciding whether they would be comfortable with your signature on a contract they have to defend. At the 411th, the SCO chairs, three to five voting members ask questions calibrated to the class you requested, the Chief of C&P facilitates without voting, and the recommendation has to be unanimous. The way to sound like a contracting officer is to answer in one repeatable structure - State, Cite, Apply, Risk, Route - in forty-five to ninety seconds, and to tell the truth when you do not know.

sections.heading: The 411th board: who is in the room and what happens
sections.body:
From the 411th CSB warrant process workflow of July 2026: the SCO chairs the CORB. Voting members are drawn from the SCO, the PD, the CoCO and/or Division Chiefs, and KOs. CONOPS and the Chief, C&P facilitate and do not vote. The board sits on the Commander's calendar the second Wednesday of each month.

On receipt of the invitation, CONOPS and C&P prepare the CORB questions, the cover sheet and the scoring sheet, generate the warrant number, and prepare the draft appointment memorandum and certificate for upload to VCE-Warrants. The SCO makes the appointment in VCE-Warrants only on a unanimous recommendation from the board members. The SCO may waive the CORB; Army policy does not permit waiving the board for an Unlimited warrant. Urgent applications may run on a shorter timeline based on mission requirements.

Policy v12 adds the general rule: the HCA or the delegated official chairs and administers the board and selects three to five additional members with a mix of experience, legal expertise and supervisory background appropriate to the warrant type. Confirm the current cadence, scoring sheet and routing with C&P before your board.

sections.heading: SCARR: the answer framework
sections.body:
One framework, used out loud, for every scenario question. State, Cite, Apply, Risk, Route.

- STATE the rule in one plain sentence, bottom line first. Not background - the rule.
- CITE the authority in layers: the RFO FAR section, then DFARS or AFARS, then statute or Army policy, then local procedure. Say 'Cite:' out loud; it signals you are done analyzing and are now sourcing.
- APPLY the rule to the facts you were given. Which conditions are met, which are not, what you still need to know. Ask at most one clarifying question rather than assuming a missing fact.
- RISK: name the real exposure - fiscal (Antideficiency Act, purpose, bona fide need), competition, performance, ethics, mission, reputational. Say what would make it worse.
- ROUTE: what you do now, what you can approve at your warrant level, and who must approve or be coordinated with - legal, the competition advocate, C&P, the SCO or HCA, the resource manager, USFK J4 for LCS, FKAQ for SOFA. Close with a one-sentence recommendation.

For a pure knowledge question use the short form - State and Cite, then stop. Do not manufacture a scenario the board did not give you.

sections.heading: Timing, structure and the sound of a good answer
sections.body:
Forty-five to ninety seconds. A clear answer with a recommendation beats a five-minute tour of the FAR, and the board will ask for more if they want more.

Answer the question asked. If it is 'how many days,' say the number first. If it is 'what would you do,' say the action first. Then supply the structure underneath.

Cite in layers and know what layer you are in. Calling an Army policy 'the FAR', citing DFARS for a statutory rule, or presenting a local threshold as if it were regulation are scored as knowledge failures, not slips.

Know the RFO numbers for the top concepts cold: ratification 1.405, COR designation 1.404, only one responsible source 6.103-1, urgency 6.103-2, justification and approval 6.104, commercial simplified procedures 12.201-1, commercial termination 12.304, price analysis 15.404-1, options 17.204-1, rule of two 19.104-1, agency protest 33.104, GAO protest 33.105, final decision 33.205-6, personal services 37.201-2, change orders 43.302, GFP liability 45.104 and 52.245-1, cure and show cause 49.402-3 and 49.607. When a board member uses an old number, answer the concept and offer the new number - politely, once.

Know the thresholds for your class and one above, and know the cumulative instrument value rule.

sections.heading: Saying 'I don't know' correctly
sections.body:
Every candidate hits a question they cannot answer. The board expects it. What they measure is what you do next, because that is what you will do at your desk with nobody watching.

The scoring reality: 'I do not know the section number, but the rule is that the contractor is not liable for loss of Government property unless one of four exceptions applies, and I would confirm the paragraph in Part 45 before I signed anything' scores a 3 or better. A confident wrong answer scores a 1 and colors every answer that follows, because the board now has to discount everything you say.

The formula: say what you know, name where the answer lives, say how you would confirm it, and stop. Do not fill the silence and do not invent a section number - a fabricated cite is the fastest way to lose a board.

Two related moves. If a scenario is missing a fact you actually need, ask for it: 'Is this O&M or LCS funded?' or 'Is this cost-type or fixed-price?' shows judgment. Ask one question, not three. If you realize mid-answer you were wrong, say so and correct it; composure is a scored dimension.

sections.heading: Follow-up probes and what they are testing
sections.body:
Probes follow your answer; they do not open a new topic. The pattern is that a board member takes your answer and changes one fact to see whether you understood the rule or memorized the outcome.

What that looks like: you explain the CICA stay and the probe moves the filing date from day four to day twelve. You explain a set-aside and the probe adds a second interested source. You explain ratification and the probe removes the funds availability.

The right reaction is to re-run the test out loud, not to defend the prior answer: 'That changes it - at day twelve the stay no longer applies, so performance continues and my focus shifts to the agency report.' Boards reward a candidate who visibly re-applies the rule.

Common probes from the board guide: how severability changes your funding answer; what market research must show before you sign a justification and who approves it; whether a contractor e-mail claiming money is a claim; who bears the loss on Government property; who awards an LCS action; what you can sign today and what you push up; and what you say when a Commander names a vendor.

sections.heading: Class-specific expectations and how you are scored
sections.body:
Questions are calibrated to the class you requested, your role and the organization's mission.

- Class I: purpose, time and amount; micro-purchase and GPC limits; simplified and commercial procedures; competition at and below the SAT; the rule of two; price reasonableness; unauthorized commitments; exclusion checks; basic ethics. Mostly knowledge with a short scenario or two.
- Class II: the above plus Part 6 exceptions and justification approval tiers, contract type and risk, options and cumulative value, severable services, ratification, COR designation, personal services limits, agency protests and the KO's role at GAO, cure and show cause, commercial terminations, change orders. At least one judgment question about saying no.
- Class III: source selection and pricing leadership - competitive range, exchanges, debriefings, price and cost analysis, cost realism, certified cost or pricing data, OCI, responsibility, subcontracting plans, claims, terminations, property. Scenarios dominate.
- Class IV: enterprise judgment - strategy, high-dollar approval routing, protests at GAO and the court, large claims, appropriation-level fiscal law, post-Government employment, leading an office. The Unlimited board cannot be waived.

The rubric weights judgment 35 percent, regulatory knowledge 30, composure 20 and communication 15, and the 411th recommendation must be unanimous.

board_angles.q: Who sits on the 411th CORB and how often does it meet?
board_angles.a: The SCO chairs, voting members come from the SCO, PD, CoCO and/or Division Chiefs and KOs, CONOPS and the Chief of C&P facilitate without voting, and it meets on the Commander's calendar the second Wednesday of each month.

board_angles.q: What happens after the board?
board_angles.a: The SCO appoints in VCE-Warrants only on a unanimous recommendation; CONOPS and C&P have already generated the warrant number and prepared the appointment memorandum and certificate for upload.

board_angles.q: You do not know the answer. What do you say?
board_angles.a: What I do know, where the answer lives, and how I would confirm it before signing - 'I do not know the section, but the rule is X and I would confirm it in Part Y' scores far better than a confident wrong cite.

board_angles.q: A board member uses a pre-RFO FAR number. What do you do?
board_angles.a: I answer the concept, then offer the current RFO number once - 'that is the sole-source exception, now at 6.103-1' - and move on without correcting them twice.

board_angles.q: How long should an answer be?
board_angles.a: Forty-five to ninety seconds: bottom line first, then state the rule, cite it, apply it to the facts, name the risk, and say who has to approve - and stop and let them probe.

board_angles.q: What is scored, and what weighs the most?
board_angles.a: Judgment at 35 percent, regulatory knowledge at 30, composure at 20 and communication at 15 - so a candidate who reasons soundly and says they would confirm a number outscores one who recites numbers but cannot decide.
